Picture someone sitting in a closed room with no phone, no computer and no door. All they have is a slot in the wall, a pen, and a pad of **order forms**. Each form has a title and a short description printed on it, like "Calendar check: tell us the machine and the date, and we'll tell you which time slots are free."

Someone outside the room (your program) slides in a student's question: "Can I use the laser cutter Thursday afternoon?" The person inside can't check anything themselves. So they pick the form whose description fits, fill in the blanks ("laser cutter, Thursday"), and slide it out. They do nothing else.

Outside, a helper reads the form, looks at the real booking calendar, and slides the result back in: "Free 1–3 pm." The person inside reads it and either replies to the student ("Yes, 1–3 pm is open") or fills in another form, such as "Book laser cutter, Thursday 1 pm." The cycle ends when they write an answer instead of a form.

Three things to take from this:

- **The model never does the action.** It only writes the request. Your code runs it.
- **The printed descriptions are how the model chooses.** A vague description means the wrong form gets picked. This is why writing tool descriptions is in your mission.
- **Results come back as plain text,** and the model just reads them.

The analogy breaks down in one place. A real person would stop and ask you if a form was confusing. The model will sometimes guess at a blank and fill it in wrongly, so your program has to check the forms it gets.

Quick check, in your own words: if the assistant books the wrong machine, what did the model do and what did your code do?

If you'd like a longer walk-through with the makerspace assistant, I can write you a lesson on it.
